extraction.name: Common Corpus
extraction.description: The largest open multilingual dataset for LLM pre-training, assembled from uncopyrighted or permissively licensed sources and totaling about two trillion tokens across text, code, scientific, cultural, government, web, and semantic data.
extraction.creator: PleIAs
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus was assembled since 2024 by aggregating six collections—Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic—from public domain or permissively licensed sources. Collection methods included collection-as-data dumps, APIs, standard retrieval methods, OpenAlex API filtering by license, reuse of existing datasets such as The Stack and The Pile, and collaborations to adapt Wikidata into natural language.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web API, Software Collection, Document analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include public-domain and permissively licensed texts, PDFs, XML, web content, code repositories, scientific papers, Wikimedia projects, YouTube transcripts, StackExchange, and Wikidata. The corpus includes sources such as OpenAlex, Stack v1/v2, Wikimedia Enterprise dumps, Internet Archive, Delpher, SEC EDGAR, WTO, AMF, and cultural heritage collections.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data were manipulated through OCR correction and rewriting, PII replacement with fictitious realistic values, toxicity filtering with removal or synthetic rewriting, and conversion of Wikidata RDF triples into formal natural-language sequences with multilingual translations concatenated by newlines.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing included text segmentation with Segmentext; OCR quality detection with OCRoscope and OCRerrcr; OCR correction with OCRonos; PII detection and replacement using Microsoft Presidio plus custom regexes; toxicity detection with Celadon; filtering by license; and for code, removing undesired file types and formats, applying manual quality filters, removing files with 75% or more digits, and normalizing line breaks before recalculating line lengths.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A separate multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon, was trained from scratch on 2 million annotated samples to identify toxic and harmful content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Microsoft Presidio, Celadon, fastText language identification model, cld2
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is an evolving resource with archived past versions on Hugging Face for reproducibility.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally identifiable information (PII), including phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses, is considered sensitive and is removed or replaced.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support open, auditable, legally compliant LLM development and open science infrastructure, while reducing reliance on copyrighted or proprietary data and enabling multilingual and creative-writing applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors note risks of harmful and biased content, especially in web data and historical public-domain texts, including racial and gender biases and outdated harmful language about ethnic groups, women, violence, and other themes. They mitigate these through toxicity filtering and rewriting, but acknowledge imperfect accuracy.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The corpus does not cover all available open data; low-resource language coverage remains shallow; 2 trillion tokens are sufficient only for limited-size models; it does not contain instruction-tuning or specialized-task data and is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning; and curation methods such as OCR correction, toxicity detection, and PII removal are not 100% accurate.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use is LLM pre-training, including fully open and auditable models. The corpus can also be used with other open datasets, for multilingual language modeling, creative writing models, historical language models, coding applications, reasoning and structured-output tasks, multimodal and vision-language models, retrieval-augmented generation, classifiers, synthetic datasets, and benchmarks. It is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning.

name.evidence: In this paper, we introduce Common Corpus1, the largest open dataset for language model pre-training.

description.evidence: In this paper, we introduce Common Corpus1, the largest open dataset for language model pre-training. The data assembled in Common Corpus are either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses and amount to about two trillion tokens. The dataset contains a wide variety of languages, ranging from the main European languages to low-resource ones rarely present in pre-training datasets; in addition, it includes a large portion of code data.

publisher.evidence: Common Corpus is available on HuggingFace as an aggregation of 10,000 parquet files

datePublished.evidence: The current version of Common Corpus, the one we describe in this paper, was released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit.

inLanguage.evidence: Common Corpus is multilingual (see Figure 1 and Table 2 for language coverage).

isLiveDataset.evidence: Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset

rai:dataCollection.evidence: In this paper, we present Common Corpus , which has been an ongoing effort since 2024... It has grown to become the largest open dataset for pre-training Large Language Models at about 2 trillion tokens... Common Corpus is available on HuggingFace as an aggregation of 10,000 parquet files and is composed of six collections: Open Govemment, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic. A large part of Open Culture is compiled from Collections As Data (CAD) — large dumps of texts, datasets, PDFs, and even raw XML output (METS/ALTO). All other parts of Open Culture have been collected on a resource-by-resource basis using APIs and other standard retrieval methods whenever available. OpenAlex maintains an expansive API search engine tracking detailed metadata for each indexed item... We filtered OpenAlex on the three following licenses: CC-By, Public Domain/CC0, and CC-By-SA. The code data we use comes from the Stack v1 and v2... We reused the version from The Pile... Thanks to a collaboration with Wikimedia Deutschland, the entire set of Wikidata has been adapted in natural language and added to Common Corpus.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: Do not capture highly sensitive data. We remove personally identifiable information from our datasets (Section 4.4). Personally Identifiable Information (PII), which is any information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual’s identity, is protected under legislation such as GDPR... there is a staggering amount of personal data in widely used datasets, e.g., large quantities of phone numbers in RedPajama, email addresses in S2ORC and peS2o, and IP addresses in the Stack

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Through the release of this dataset, we show that open LLM research and development is possible while meeting legal and regulatory requirements—even in the EU, where AI regulations are currently the strictest... Common Corpus aims to support the pre-training of fully open and auditable LLMs... Beyond the main dataset, Common Corpus works as an open science infrastructure dedicated to the entire lifecycle of language models.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: In addition to posing legal and regulatory issues, web data is a major source of harmful and biased content (Common Crawl was shown to contain sexual content, hate speech, and racial and gender biases... ). Public Domain data... Many texts there are historical periodicals and monographs from at least 80 years ago. Cultural norms surrounding the discussion of certain ethnic groups, women, and themes such as violence have changed dramatically. Many of these texts, therefore, do not meet modem ethical standards. Training models on these texts would lead to the reproduction and circulation of harmful language... Even though we used these methods responsibly and mitigated many issues overlooked by the counterparts... none of the curation methods could naturally facilitate a hundred-percent accuracy.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Common Corpus is far from collecting the whole range of available open data... even though the language diversity of the data is large, the coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow... the amount of collected data (2 trillion tokens) is suitable for pre-training of models of limited size... Larger models, however will require significantly larger amounts of data. In addition, Common Corpus naturally does not contain data for instruction-tuning and any forms of specialized tasks. Therefore, it is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning... none of the curation methods could naturally facilitate a hundred-percent accuracy.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: In this paper, we introduce Common Corpus1, the largest open dataset for language model pre-training... Common Corpus can be used on its own or in conjunction with existing open datasets, according to one’s needs and the desired use case of a language model.
